items.content:
Trust in Procurement isn't built in the boardroom.

I mapped Procurement onto the human heart. 

Every chamber, valve and vessel has a job. So does every habit that earns you trust.

Sinoatrial Node - The Trust Pacemaker 
↳ Sets the rhythm every other beat follows. 
↳ Trust isn't a big gesture. It's showing up on time, replying when you said you would, and doing that on repeat until the rhythm sets itself.

Capillaries - The Micro-Trust Network 
↳ The smallest vessels, where the real exchange happens. 
↳ Not the big meetings. The quick reply. The favour returned. The heads-up given before it was owed.

Miss those two and nothing else in the system works. You can have the strongest negotiation chamber in the business. 

If the rhythm's off and the small exchanges don't happen, stakeholders won't wait around to find out why.

Right Atrium - The Feedback Intake
↳ Supplier complaints, stakeholder frustration, hard feedback lands here first. ↳ The discipline is processing it. Not deflecting it.

Left Atrium - The Empathy Reservoir 
↳ The pause before responding. 
↳ Actually absorbing what someone's telling you before you react to it.

Left Ventricle - The Negotiation Chamber 
↳ The strongest chamber, pumping with the most force. 
↳ Built on preparation, leverage, and knowing your walk-away point before you sit down.

Mitral Valve - The Boundary Valve 
↳ Opens to let the right requests through. Closes to stop scope creep flowing back. 
↳ Saying no cleanly is still a form of trust.

Septum - The Integrity Wall 
↳ Keeps the two sides completely separate so nothing crosses that shouldn't. ↳ The line you don't cross under pressure, even for a good supplier relationship.

Aorta - The Value Artery 
↳ The single channel your value travels through to reach the C-suite. 
↳ Do the work brilliantly and say nothing about it, and it still won't get funded next year.

The muscle, the valves, the arteries all matter. But none of them work without rhythm.

Trust isn't the big win you post about. It's the small thing you did again today.

Any others you'd add to the heart?

items.content:
Procurement leaders breathe dashboards.

The infographic shows 6 dashboards for procurement teams:

# 1 - Spend by Category Dashboard
↳ A dashboard that shows total spend by category, supplier group, or business unit.
 ↳ Instantly reveals where the money, leverage, and risk really sit

# 2 - Supplier Onboarding Efficiency Tracker
↳ Track average supplier set-up time year on year
↳ Spot process friction early and remove delays before they block delivery

# 3 - Spend Trend Dashboard
↳ Visualise monthly spend patterns across the year
↳ Identify seasonality, abnormal spikes, and budget drift before Finance flags it

# 4 - Procurement ROI Dashboard
↳ Compare procurement ROI against benchmark and cost of the function
↳ Answer the exec-level question: “Is procurement worth the investment?”

# 5 - Cost Savings vs Cost Avoidance Report
↳ Separate realised savings from avoided future costs
↳ Show total financial impact, not just negotiated wins

# 6 - Active Contract & Supplier Performance Dashboard
↳ Track active suppliers, % contracted, SLAs monitored, and partner tiers
↳ Shift supplier management from admin to real risk and value control

Any others to add?

items.content:
Most people accidentally discover what procurement is really about.

Because nobody tells them.

Universities don’t teach it.
 Job descriptions don’t explain it.
 And most procurement careers are built through trial and error.

The reality?

The job is very different from what most people expect.

7 things nobody tells you about procurement:

1/ It’s a commercial function, not an admin one.

Yet you’ll spend years proving that to people who should already know. The best procurement professionals don’t process requests. They influence business outcomes.

2/ The politics are real.

Supplier decisions get overridden. Stakeholders have favourites. Budget holders have agendas. Technical capability matters, but learning how organisations really work matters just as much.

3/ Soft skills beat technical skills.

You can know every clause in the contract. Every sourcing methodology. Every procurement process.
None of it matters if you can’t build trust, influence decisions and bring people with you.

4/ Your suppliers know more than you think.

They’ve seen your competitors. They’ve seen other industries. They’ve seen what works and what fails.
The smartest procurement professionals treat suppliers as a source of market intelligence.

5/ Speed and compliance pull in opposite directions.

The business wants things faster. Procurement wants things controlled.
Your job is to find the balance.
And somehow you’ll often get blamed from both directions.

6/ The value you create is often invisible.

The crisis that never happened. The supplier failure that was avoided. The cost increase that never materialised.
Nobody celebrates what didn’t go wrong.

7/ The career path is wider than most people realise.

CPO. Consultant. Founder. COO. Commercial leader.

The skills you develop in procurement transfer far beyond procurement itself.

Most procurement professionals spend years learning these lessons the hard way.

The lucky ones learn them early. 

I probably learned many of the lessons too late to save me from some real dips in confidence and episodes of anxiety. 

This is why it’s now my life’s work to help procurement professionals globally to learn these lessons. 

Know you are not alone.


Which one do you think is underestimated the most. 

Pick a number 1 to 7 and let me know in the comments 👇

items.content:
Procurement gets overcomplicated. It doesn't need to.

This infographic shows 5 frameworks that can be applied to most scenariosL

↳ SWOT Analysis - maps internal strengths and weaknesses against external opportunities and threats 

↳ PESTLE Analysis - reads the external forces shaping your category (political, economic, social, technical, legal, environmental) 

↳ SCOR Framework - connects procurement to the end-to-end supply chain. Useful for maturity assessments and transformation work 

↳ SIPOC Framework - maps suppliers, inputs, processes, outputs, and customers to surface inefficiencies and process gaps 

↳ RACI Matrix - removes ambiguity over who owns what, so decisions actually get made

Simple frameworks. Wide application. Worth knowing cold.

Btw...I stole this excellent framework summary from Tanya W. with her full permission. I've just rebranded it and added my own take. Everyone should follow Tanya.

items.content:
Many say the RFP process is "used to get the best possible price". 

I'm sorry. It’s not. Even Wikipedia is wrong.

I don’t like semantic battles

And I know many in Procurement are being tasked with cutting costs for Q3 of 2026

Particularly with the continued bleak economic forecasts and widely held viewpoint that AI can drive efficiency savings. 

But if you employ that approach to assess outcomes, the most likely long term one for your business is failure.

So, what exactly is an RFP used for? 

RFP is short for “Request for Proposal.” 

But perhaps it should be rebadged as “Request for Partnership”.

The goal of an RFP is to evaluate multiple options and get the maximum return on any investment your business makes.

It's about learning what’s available as efficiently and objectively as possible. 

Maximising value while minimising risk. 

Not creating a low cost MVP solution for your business.

The evaluation stages of an RFP often cause greatest confusion. 

Once the RFP has been sent to suppliers, many evaluate the responses based on pre conceived criteria of ‘what good looks like’.

And the worst go on to over inflate the importance of cost while completely dismissing the significance of value.

In a Vendr interview here https://lnkd.in/g9S86SKH

re-evaluation of key performance indicators (KPIs) is discussed, particularly the shift away from focusing solely on cost savings.

Dr. Elouise Epstein advocates for using revenue as a more effective guiding metric and turning cost centres into profit centres where possible. 

Another approach I heard recently and loved is using the term "solutions workshops," rather than supplier or product demos when it comes to the presentations in an RFP.

The emphasis being on collaborating with suppliers to learn and develop understanding

Rather than pitching suppliers against each other in a race of doom to the bottom.

items.content:
When you treat procurement as a process, you lose every strategic advantage it could give you.

Let's be honest.

Every business says procurement is "a strategic partner."

But most procurement teams would tell a different story.

The truth?

Procurement's status isn't what leadership says it is.

It's what procurement experiences daily.

6 green flags that separate great procurement teams from the rest:

1/ Procurement is in the room before decisions are made.

The business doesn't bring you in to rubber-stamp a supplier they've already chosen. Early involvement is the clearest signal that procurement is trusted. Not just processed.

2/ The CPO has a seat at the leadership table.

Not buried in Finance. Not three layers removed from the CEO. Where procurement sits in the org chart tells you exactly how seriously the business takes it.

3/ Procurement is measured on value. Not just savings.

Risk reduced. Supplier innovation unlocked. Business outcomes delivered. A business that only measures procurement on cost reduction is asking it to stay tactical forever.

4/ Stakeholders come to procurement voluntarily.

They don't ask "do I have to involve procurement?" They ask "can procurement help with this?" When the business comes to you before it has to, you've become a partner. Not a process.

5/ Procurement has a real development budget.

Tools. Training. Headcount. Career development that reflects strategic importance. A business serious about procurement invests in it. Lip service doesn't come with a budget line.

6/ The business understands what bypassing procurement costs them.

Not as a policy threat. As a shared understanding. When stakeholders self-police maverick spend, procurement has genuinely changed the culture.

Most procurement leaders overestimate where they stand.

They look at the policies. The job titles. The "strategic" label on the org chart.

But none of that matters if the business still treats procurement as the team you go to last.
Status isn't built in policy documents.

It's built in the small moments. The early invites. The unsolicited "can you help us with this?" The maverick spend that doesn't happen.

Your business is showing you everything.

What are you seeing?

items.content:
Most procurement teams don't get recognised for cost avoidance

and yet they spend most of their time

- deflecting price increases
- challenging spend requests for services that aren't needed
- mitigating risks that could cost the company millions

I know, I've been there.

Fighting for credit and struggling to justify my existence, despite the huge sums I KNOW the company avoided because of procurement being a thing. 

Cost Reduction and Cost Avoidance are similar but they're not the same.

I'd argue Cost Avoidance is our bigger and more important job, but it's the part that largely goes unnoticed...

until your organisation decides they don't need procurement of course, because you weren't able to show the numbers on a tracker

or because finance didn't believe the numbers you provided

or because (cough) A.I. can do it all now. 

In this infographic, I show you how to do it, the differences between the two and the key skills required.

___

1. Cost Reduction
2. Cost Avoidance

Bonus points if you're able to provide rationale.

Triple bonus points if you don't use AI to comment 🙂.

items.content:
Most procurement teams are managing spend wrong. 

(And don't know which category costs the most.)

The challenge: 

Every pound leaving your business falls into one of four buckets. And each one demands a different approach.

DIRECT SPEND - "Cost of Production" 
↳ Raw materials, components, packaging
↳ The spend that directly builds what you sell 
↳ Miss this? Your gross margin disappears overnight

INDIRECT SPEND - "Cost of Running the Business" 
↳ IT, facilities, marketing, travel and office supplies 
↳ Spread across every department, often completely unmanaged 
↳ Ignore this? Maverick spend quietly drains your EBITDA

SERVICES SPEND - "Cost of Expertise" 
↳ Consulting firms, legal, IT partners, interim contractors 
↳ Bought for outcomes, usually paid for activity 
↳ No clear scope? Watch invoices spiral out of control

CAPEX SPEND - "Cost of Assets & Investment" 
↳ Manufacturing equipment, facilities, major tech platforms 
↳ Capitalised on the balance sheet, depreciated over time 
↳ Get the supplier wrong? You're locked into that mistake for years

Let's look at 2 examples:

Manufacturing Business:
• Direct: £2M/year (steel, components, packaging)
• Indirect: £500K/year (IT software, facilities management)
• Services: £300K/year (engineering consultants, legal)
• CapEx: £1.5M once (new production line)

Professional Services Firm:
• Direct: Minimal (people are the product)
• Indirect: £800K/year (office space, technology, HR)
• Services: £200K/year (specialist subcontractors, legal)
• CapEx: £400K once (proprietary software platform)

Most procurement teams lump everything into one "spend" bucket. Then wonder why they can't find savings.

But when you separate them?

Direct → Conduct should-cost analysis & protect gross margin 
Indirect → Consolidate suppliers & drive contract compliance 
Services → Define scope clearly & link payment to outcomes 
CapEx → Evaluate total lifecycle cost, not just purchase price

Crucial insights: 

✓ High Direct Spend? Strategic sourcing & supplier partnerships are non-negotiable 
✓ Unmanaged Indirect? Maverick spend is quietly killing your EBITDA 
✓ Rising Services costs? You've got scope creep & weak governance 
✓ Poor CapEx decisions? You'll feel the pain on the balance sheet for years

Common traps: 

❌ Focusing on price rather than total cost 
❌ Applying the same strategy to every spend category 
❌ Weak stakeholder engagement across business functions 
❌ No spend visibility to even know where the real problem is

When you finally understand your spend categories?

You negotiate with confidence. 
You build strategy by category, not gut feel. 
You become a procurement function the business respects.

Stop managing "expenses." 
Start managing Direct, Indirect, Services & CapEx spend.

That's how procurement creates real business value.

YouTube is a University for Procurement 

But it’s hard to cut through the noise.

Top 10 channels worth a subscribe:


1. Zerite Network https://lnkd.in/ey-B8SyS

I cannot tell you how good this one is. The channel offers in-depth tutorials, lectures, and how-tos about Procurement, online learning, financial planning, business start-up, CPA lectures, and ACCA tutorials. 


2. The World of Procurement https://lnkd.in/e8JNtJaE

Daniel Barnes needs no introduction. Lots of superb quality how to videos on Contract Management and Procurement but now with areal slant on AI. This man truly is an expert when it comes to understanding the power of AI in procurement. 

***************************************

Btw. If you want to be one of the first to subscribe and support my Procurement Protagonist YouTube here's where to go 🙂 👇 

https://lnkd.in/eAzJR_pn

For free procurement advice and the odd entertaining rant too! 

***************************************


3. Dual Source Discord https://lnkd.in/ehMjqxaG

Procurement with Personality with a capital 'P'. I've learned about Networking, Procurement conferences, Procurement Travel Tips, LinkedIn. 
You name in, they have it covered. 


4. Let’s talk Supply Chain https://lnkd.in/e3vUZ7AA

I met Sarah Barnes-Humphrey at DPW Amsterdam. She’s great. Lots of great interviews on Supply Chain and a real focus on women in the profession.


5. Procurement Tactics https://lnkd.in/e6qm5K2s

Plenty of good coaching content in really easily digestible clips. All the fundamentals of procurement are here and the content is regularly kept up to date. 


6. CIPS https://lnkd.in/efXj67Uc

This is actually pretty good. If you fight through the videos where they are celebrating CIPS there’s some really informative videos. I’ve never understood why CIPS don’t make more of their Digital content. 


7. Supply Chain Doctrine https://lnkd.in/emS-98xP

Loads of educational resources on various aspects of supply chain management, from procurement and inventory management to warehouse management, store management, distribution management, green supply chain and general management.


8. Wonder Services https://lnkd.in/ed3yQiVF

A great channel for any business or Procurement team looking to drive transformation, digital, organisational or anything else with a focus on how to bring your people along.


9. SCMDOJO https://lnkd.in/eG6n5wMB

On demand Supply Chain Knowledge Content & Expertise. This is a great resource for anyone looking for tips to help solve the problems they face in their jobs and business. This is a one stop knowledge bank.


10. The Art of Procurement https://lnkd.in/eJfVzYHz

There is so much content here and it's the best place for up to date content -  nearly 1000 videos. It's like a Procurement daily news channel that supports their claim they aim to 10x the impact of Procurement.

What have I missed?

items.content:
How to shift procurement to strategic. Free Guide 🎁 

Perception is built on evidence. But the evidence the business sees every day is tactical.

Let's look at the transformation step by step:

1️⃣ Signs the business sees you as tactical

↳ They only involve you AFTER a supplier has been chosen 
↳ Stakeholders treat procurement as a box-ticking exercise 
↳ You're only measured on cost savings 
↳ You spend more time on POs than influencing decisions 
↳ Nobody invites you to early planning conversations 
↳ Your reports go to Finance, not the boardroom 
↳ The business regularly goes around procurement entirely

If 3+ are true, you're seen as purchasing. Not procurement.


2️⃣ The 5 shifts to close the gap

(i) From Price to Value 
↳ Stop leading with "we got 10% off" 
↳ Start showing total cost of ownership, risk reduction, supplier reliability

(ii) From Reactive to Proactive 
↳ Stop waiting to be briefed after decisions are made 
↳ Start building relationships that get you upstream

(iii) From Process Enforcer to Business Partner 
↳ Stop saying "you need to follow the procurement process" 
↳ Start saying "let's figure out how to get you the outcome you need"

(iv) From Tactical KPIs to Strategic Metrics 
↳ Stop reporting PO cycle times and savings vs budget 
↳ Start reporting supplier risk, value delivered, market benchmarks

(v) From Departmental to Cross-Functional 
↳ Stop talking only to direct budget holders 
↳ Start building relationships with Finance, Legal, Operations, and the C-suite


3️⃣ Change how you speak

Instead of: "You should have involved us earlier" ❌ 
Try: "At what point did the supplier conversation start?" ✅ 

Instead of: "That's not the procurement process" ❌ 
Try: "Let's see how we can make this work safely" ✅ 

Instead of: "We need 3 quotes" ❌ 
Try: "Here's what the market looks like. Let me show you the options" ✅ 

Instead of: "I can't approve that supplier" ❌ 
Try: "There are some risks here. Let's talk through them" ✅ 

Instead of: "We saved £200K this quarter" ❌ 
Try: "We reduced cost AND improved delivery reliability by 15%" ✅ 


4️⃣ The perception checklist

↳ Do stakeholders involve you before supplier decisions? 
↳ Do you have relationships with senior leaders beyond direct contacts? 
↳ Can you articulate procurement's value beyond savings? 
↳ Do you bring market intelligence, not just process? 
↳ Does the business know what it costs to bypass procurement? 
↳ Are your KPIs linked to business strategy? 
↳ Does procurement have a voice in supplier innovation?

The gap isn't about capability. It's about visibility, language & how procurement shows up.

items.content:
5 ways AI is making procurement leaders obsolete.

And what we can do about it, starting today.

AI is no longer automating only administrative work.

It is moving into the work we once called “strategic.”

Here are five examples:

1. Risk management

AI can identify emerging risks, assess exposure, and find alternatives in seconds.

Many teams are still chasing suppliers for updates.

2. Negotiation

AI can model scenarios, predict responses, and recommend the next move.

Many leaders still rely on what worked last year.

3. Opportunity identification

AI can uncover savings, innovation, and value opportunities hidden across thousands of data points.

Humans often see only what they already know to look for.

4. Governance

Approvals, compliance checks, and supplier-performance reviews increasingly happen automatically.

Being the person who controls the process creates less value.

5. Demand anticipation

AI can predict needs before the business formally raises them.

Traditional sourcing can look slow before it even begins.

Here is the uncomfortable truth.

If your value comes from approving, reporting, checking, and chasing, AI is learning your job.

The leaders who remain relevant will play a different role.

They will:

• Orchestrate stakeholders around enterprise outcomes
• Make decisions when the data remains incomplete
• Build trust across complex ecosystems
• Coach teams to think beyond the process
• Turn technology into measurable business advantage

AI does not eliminate procurement leadership.

It raises the standard for what leadership must become.

The gatekeeper is becoming obsolete.

The enterprise force multiplier is only getting started.

items.content:
I just gifted myself something that cost $30.

It could help me earn $30,000 or more. 

No, it isn’t an AI gadget or an investing app.

It’s a phone lockbox.

Like many people, I average 5–6 hours of screen time every day.

The real cost isn’t just the hours.

It’s the constant interruptions.
The fragmented focus.
The moments with family when my attention is only half there.

So I decided to stop relying on willpower.

Instead, I changed my environment.

This little box locks away my phone for a set period of time.

The best part, I can’t unlock it before the timer runs off. 

If it helps me reduce my screen time by just 20–30%, the return could be enormous:

• More deep, uninterrupted thinking.
• Better decisions at work.
• More meaningful conversations with my wife and kids.
• More books read.
• More time creating instead of consuming.

We often invest thousands of dollars in improving our skills.

Maybe protecting our attention delivers an even higher return.

What’s the best under-$50 purchase that’s had an outsized impact on your life?

items.content:
I killed my evening doomscroll habit saving 1-2 hours.

From ONE simple habit:

Switching my phone screen to grayscale.

You don't have to be highly disciplined or have iron willpower to break the doomscroll habit.

Instead, use this simple 30-second habit:

(It's how I consistently stay off my phone after 9pm every single day.)

Go to Settings. Accessibility. Display filters. Turn on grayscale.

That's it. Your phone still works. You just stripped out the color.

This makes the next evening's wind-down effortless for 3 reasons:

1. Color is what makes apps addictive.

Every red notification, every bright thumbnail is engineered to trigger dopamine. Grayscale removes that trigger entirely. The apps look flat. Boring. Easy to ignore.

2. Your brain stops linking your phone to reward.

Repeat this enough nights and the association breaks. Phone in hand no longer means pleasure. It just means a gray screen you don't really want to look at.

3. You put it down sooner because it's less interesting.

No willpower needed. No app blocker. No timer. The phone just stops competing for your attention because it stopped being visually stimulating.

What's one small change you've made that actually stuck?

items.content:
What do Procurement and Emi Martinez have in common?

More than you think.

Martinez blocked 12 shots in the final against Spain. Including that miracle save with seconds left.

Nobody talks about those. All anyone remembers is the one shot that got past him. Even though it wasn't his fault.

Procurement works the same way.

You prevent disasters. You keep costs down. You make risk disappear. But most of it stays invisible. No applause for the fires you put out. No recognition for the losses that never happen.

Stakeholders forget the twelve problems you solved. They only notice the one you couldn't stop.

The metrics always focus on what goes wrong, never what you quietly fix in the background.

One miss overshadows a dozen saves.

That's the reality.

If you are a procurement leader, remember this:

Your team can't win without you.

You won't hear the cheers. You won't see your name in lights. But every smooth handoff, every avoided disaster, every quiet save, those are your fingerprints.

The crowd only sees the scoreboard. They miss the work behind the scenes.

Don't chase applause. Focus on impact.

Your wins might be invisible, but they're what keeps the business moving.

Tag someone who may benefit from this reminder.

items.content:
Joe had an offer in hand, ready to resign.

One career conversation changed what happened next.

Joe is fictional.

But I have seen versions of his story many times.

He was a strong performer.

Respected by his colleagues.

Successful in his role.

But something was missing.

Before informing his manager, he reached out to a mentor.

Out of courtesy.

Maybe for perspective.

I appreciated the trust.

So instead of asking him why he wanted to leave, we explored something deeper.

His six fundamental human needs.

Certainty.

Was he looking for more stability?

No.

Variety.

Was he bored and looking for something different?

Not really.

Connection.

Did he feel disconnected from his team?

No.

Then we got to significance.

And something clicked.

Joe wanted to feel that he mattered.

He wanted his leadership to be recognized.

The bigger title in the new company represented that.

Then we explored growth.

He felt he had stopped learning.

The new role promised a bigger challenge.

Finally, contribution.

Joe wanted to make a bigger impact.

He believed the new company would give him that opportunity.

Suddenly, the problem became clearer.

Joe was not simply leaving for a bigger title.

Three important needs were not being met:

Significance.

Growth.

Contribution.

So I asked him one more question.

“Is leaving the only way to meet them?”

Maybe not.

Joe decided not to resign.

At least, not yet.

Instead, he would have a different career conversation with his manager.

Not:

“When will I get promoted?”

But:

“How can I expand my leadership, keep growing, and contribute at a higher level?”

Maybe there was a bigger role he could play.

A new challenge he could take on.

A team he could lead.

A problem he could own.

Even without an immediate promotion.

Perhaps Joe would still decide to leave.

And that might be the right decision.

But at least he would be solving the real problem.

This fictional story makes me wonder:

How many regrettable losses happen because we start the career conversation only after someone resigns?

By then, the conversation may already be too late.

If you know someone who could benefit from this conversation before it is too late, tag them.

items.content:
Time for the next performance review?

You may have used CAR. Now try CARE.

Most performance reviews sound like reruns.

You followed the CAR playbook.

Context. Actions. Results.

That gets you on the scoreboard.

But if you want to stand out, you need CARE.

Context. Actions. Results. Edge.

The Edge isn't just a bonus line at the end. It's not just some extra flair for the results section.

Sometimes the Edge is hidden in the context.

Maybe you tackled an assignment everyone else ran from. You stepped into a mess, not a clean slate.

Maybe your action was the Edge.

You broke the old process. Or you convinced the one stakeholder nobody else could reach. Or you skipped the obvious route and found a smarter way.

Sometimes the Edge comes in the results.

You didn't just hit the target. You changed the target. You made the solution scalable. Or you created new possibilities nobody even asked for.

The Edge can show up anywhere in your story.

But you have to call it out.

Don't let it get lost between bullet points.

Anyone can tell a CAR story.

But when you nail the Edge, you become unforgettable.

Next performance review, look closer.

Where's the Edge in your context, your actions, your results?

Spell it out.

CARE beats CAR every time.

Give them a reason to remember you.

items.content:
I am often asked what did I gain/lose after moving to the US.

I gained a lifelong lesson. I lost my superhero cape.

For years, I thought working late was commitment.

Being the last person to leave was dedication.

Being available whenever someone needed me was leadership.

Then I moved to the US.

The change wasn't my choice. It was forced.

Most evenings, I had somewhere I needed to be.

Ira's Taekwondo.

Anaya's tennis.

Groceries to pick up.

A family commitment.

I couldn't rely on staying late to get everything done anymore.
And I didn't have house help or a support system.

So I had to change how I worked.

Prioritize harder.

Delegate more.

Trust people more.

Say no more often.

And focus my time where only I could add value.

Something unexpected happened.

I didn't become less effective.

I became more effective.

It made me question something I'd believed for years:

Sometimes, working long hours isn't commitment.

It's a sign we haven't built a system that works without our heroics.

I still work late when it truly matters.

But I don't wear it as a badge of honor.

Leadership isn't about being the hero.

It's about building a team that doesn't need one.

items.content:
What if today was your last day? Or first day?

What if it was both?

Would you live differently?
Would you love differently?

Now flip the question.

What if today was your first day?

Would you learn differently?
Would you lead differently?

We rarely know when something is our last.

The last conversation.
The last meeting.
The last ordinary dinner with someone we love.

And yet, we often live as if there will always be another.

We also forget that every morning can be a first.

A first chance to listen differently.
To learn something new.
To lead without yesterday’s assumptions.

Maybe we need both perspectives.

Live like it could be your last day.

With gratitude.
With presence.
With love.

Lead like it is your first day.

With curiosity.
With humility.
With courage.

Hold on to what matters.

Stay open to what is possible.

items.content:
I time travelled 20 years forward and backward. 

And learnt a life lesson I can’t wait to share. 

Here are 3 things I complain about now, but my future self will miss.

And my younger self dreamed about them.

1. Family chaos  
The constant noise, the mess, the endless questions. It drives me nuts. But 20 years ago, I wanted this life. In another 20, the silence will sting.

2. Work pressure  
Back-to-back meetings, deadlines, everyone needing something. Annoying now. But I used to want to matter. I'll miss feeling in demand when nobody is calling.

3. No free time  
Always wishing for a break. But when I had nothing but time, I wanted purpose. Soon, I'll have the time, but not the same energy.

Careful what you wish away. Today's stress is tomorrow's nostalgia.

What will you miss about today's mess?

items.content:
"Good job on cost savings."

It took me far too long to see it as a sign of trouble. 

I realized something. Whenever I focused only on cost savings, I felt invisible.

The big conversations happened without me.
Strategy, growth, market moves... procurement wasn't even in the room.

It wasn't about working harder.
It was about being relevant.

Here's what changed for me:
I stopped reporting how much money we saved.
I started speaking the language of business outcomes.

Revenue protection.
Faster launches.
Supplier-driven innovation.
Risk management that made expansion possible.

The shift didn't happen overnight.
But suddenly, the C-suite started listening.
They brought me into calls about growth, not just compliance.
They asked me for ideas, not just approvals.

Lesson for any procurement leader:
If you only talk about cost, you'll always be seen as a cost.
But when you show how procurement drives the business, you stop being invisible.

You become necessary.
